question: to the Commission Wouter Beke (PPE) Subject:

The European citric acid sector is in a precarious situation owing to ongoing dumping practices by third countries, particularly China. European producers are facing import prices that are significantly below production costs, which seriously undermines the sector’s viability. The European market for citric acid and citrates amounts to approximately 600 kilotons per year, while the combined production capacity of the remaining European producers is in the region of 350 kilotons (roughly 58 % of demand). Nevertheless, an estimated 60 % of the market is made up of Chinese imports, which indicates that there is a structural disruption in terms of market balance. The existing anti-dumping procedure is too slow and not effective enough. Although the problem has been acute since 2023, any potential adjustment to the measures is not expected until next year at the earliest. This poses a threat to the very existence of European production capacity in a strategic sector, which would have consequences for essential value chains. Against this backdrop, questions arise regarding the need for additional and faster protective measures. 1.
Is the Commission prepared to set import quotas to prevent market disruption?
What is the Commission’s position on imposing minimum local content requirements with a view to strengthening strategic anchoring and security of supply?
Is the Commission considering reintroducing minimum import prices (MIPs) for citric acid, and within what timeframe?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.6.2026) The existing anti-dumping measures on citric acid from China are in force since 2008. They are currently subject to an expiry review investigation initiated on 14 April 20261. The scope of an expiry review is to assess if there is a likelihood of continuation and/or recurrence of dumping and injury and therefore, if the measures need to be renewed for further five years. No amendment of the level and form of the measures is possible in this proceeding. Therefore, imports quotas or minimum import prices will not be considered in the proceeding. The Commission has no immediate plans to impose minimum content requirements for citric acid. Nonetheless, the Commission is exploring whether minimum content requirements for bio-based products, including citric acid, should be part of the ‘Biotech Act 2’ proposal, which is scheduled for publication by the end of 2026.
